pais.texto:
Singapore is an island the size of a large city: the city is the country. It has four official languages: English, Mandarin, Malay and Tamil.
Many Singaporeans speak two Englishes: formal English at school and at work, and Singlish, the English of the street, with friends.

lesson.introText: Today, we’ll talk about Singapore. We’ll take a look at Singlish, hawker centres and life in a city-state.
lesson.introSub: Singlish, hawker centres and life in a city-state

warmup.question: What images come to your mind when you think of Singapore?
Can a country the size of a city be successful? How?

fotos.texto: Halls with many stalls selling cheap food. Tip: a packet of tissues on the table means “taken”!
Poached chicken with rice cooked in the stock. It is often called the national dish.
Crab in a chilli and tomato sauce, eaten with fried buns.
A traditional breakfast: toast with kaya (a coconut and egg jam), soft-boiled eggs and kopi.
Chinatown, Little India and Kampong Glam: three neighbourhoods with three heritages, Chinese, Indian and Malay.
In Singapore, eating and drinking on the metro is not allowed, and littering gets you a fine.

lesson.vocabSub: words you will hear in Singapore · pay attention to pronunciation

languageGame.question: At a hawker centre, a packet of tissues on the table means “taken”.
In Singapore, you can eat and drink on the metro.
Kaya toast is a traditional dinner.
Hainanese chicken rice is often called the national dish.

conversation.question: Since the 1980s, school lessons in Singapore have been taught in English, and each student also studies their own “mother tongue”. What are the pros and cons of this system?
Should Brazilian schools teach some subjects in English? Why (not)?
The government campaigned against Singlish for decades, but people learned to switch between the two Englishes. Should governments try to control how people speak?
Several Singlish words are already in the Oxford English Dictionary. Who decides what “correct” English is?
Many Singaporeans hold two versions of a language and know when each one belongs. Can you do the same in Portuguese? Give examples.
“Kiasu” is the fear of falling behind, of missing out on something. Is this feeling common among people your age? Why?
Hawker culture became UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2020. Which Brazilian food tradition deserves this recognition? Why?
Singapore has strict rules: no eating on the metro and fines for littering. Do strict rules make a city better, or do they limit freedom?
Singapore mixes Chinese, Malay and Indian heritage. What are the benefits and the challenges of a multicultural society?
Singapore is about 730 km², a little bigger than Taubaté, with about six million people. Would you like to live in such a crowded place? Why (not)?
Food is part of national identity in Singapore. What does Brazilian food say about Brazil?

evaluation.question: Did you enjoy talking about Singapore?
Which other countries would you like to learn more about?
